This tutorial runs HyperCom on 1,000 mouse heart cells and shows how to:

1. check your input,
2. run the whole analysis with one call,
3. read the ranked ligand-receptor pairs,
4. score and plot the cells that send and receive a signal,
5. run large data (time, memory, runs that stop).

The last section runs each step on its own, for those who want to see how HyperCom works. The plots need the ggplot2 and ggridges
packages; without them the plots are skipped.

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(HyperCom)
library(dplyr)
library(Matrix)
library(tidyr)
has.ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly=TRUE)
has.ggridges <- has.ggplot2 && requireNamespace("ggridges", quietly=TRUE)
```

## 1. Check your input
HyperCom needs three inputs. Most failed runs come from one of them, so check them first.

| Input | What it must be |
|---|---|
| **Counts** | A genes x cells matrix (sparse or dense). Row names are gene symbols; column names are cell names. Raw or normalized, **never scaled**: HyperCom only uses whether each gene is above 0 in each cell. |
| **Cell metadata** | A data frame with one row per cell; row names are the cell names. A **sample** column (library or replicate) and, optionally, a **group** column (condition). |
| **Ligand-receptor database** | `cellchat.hs.lrdb` for human (genes like `TGFB1`) or `cellchat.mm.lrdb` for mouse (`Tgfb1`). |

Also:

- **Cell names must be unique.** When you merge samples, add the sample name to each barcode.
- **Cells are compared only within their sample**, so each sample needs at least 2 cells that express a ligand or receptor gene.
  One sample? Add `metadata$sample <- "all"`.
- Cells in the counts but not in the metadata are left out, with a warning.

### The example data
A 1,000-cell subset of the heart failure data of [Alexanian et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03674-1): hearts
after sham surgery (SHAM) or transverse aortic constriction (TAC), with log-normalized counts. It comes with the package as
`alexanian2021.counts` and `alexanian2021.metadata`.
```{r}
counts <- alexanian2021.counts
dim(counts)
head(rownames(counts))
head(colnames(counts))
```

```{r}
cell.meta <- alexanian2021.metadata
head(cell.meta)
table(cell.meta$sample, cell.meta$condition)
```

```{r, eval=has.ggplot2, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(cell.meta, aes(x=UMAP_1, y=UMAP_2, colour=celltype)) +
  geom_point(size=0.5) +
  theme_classic()
```

The data is mouse, so we use the mouse database. Each row is one interaction: its name, the ligand, then the receptor genes (`NA`
when the receptor has fewer subunits).
```{r}
lrdb <- cellchat.mm.lrdb
dim(lrdb)
head(lrdb, 2)
```

## 2. Run HyperCom
One call runs the whole analysis.

- HyperCom uses one thread per physical core (`threads` sets the number; `threads=1` runs on one thread).
- `significance=TRUE` adds p-values; `seed` makes them reproducible.

```{r}
outdir <- file.path(tempdir(), "overview")
res <- HyperCom(lrdb=lrdb, counts=counts, metadata=cell.meta, sample="sample",
                group="condition", significance=TRUE, seed=1,
                outdir=outdir, verbose=FALSE)
```

`res` holds the results, and they are also saved to `outdir` (`outdir=NULL` saves nothing):

| File | Contents | In `res` |
|---|---|---|
| `0.counts.rds` | counts of the ligand and receptor genes | |
| `1.lrs.csv` | interactions whose genes are all expressed | `res$lrs` |
| `2.hyperedges.csv` | hyperedges of the hypergraph | |
| `3.adj.rds` | adjacency matrix | `res$adj` |
| `4.infMat.rds` | influence matrix | `res$infMat` |
| `5.metadata.csv` | metadata of cells and genes | `res$metadata` |
| `6.priority/priority.<weight>.csv` | ranked pairs, one file per weight | `res$priority` |

Read the CSV files with `read.csv` and the `.rds` files with `readRDS` (after `library(HyperCom)`).
```{r}
list.files(outdir, recursive=TRUE)
```

### From a Seurat object or SingleCellExperiment
Same arguments, but HyperCom reads the counts and metadata from the object. `sample`, `group` and `keep` name columns of its cell
metadata (`seurat[[]]` or `colData(sce)`).
```{r, eval=FALSE}
res <- HyperCom_seurat(seurat=seurat_object, lrdb=cellchat.mm.lrdb, sample="sample",
                       group="condition", outdir="overview")
res <- HyperCom_sce(sce=sce_object, lrdb=cellchat.mm.lrdb, sample="sample",
                    group="condition", outdir="overview")
```

- **`HyperCom_seurat`** reads the `counts` layer of the `RNA` assay by default (change with `assay` and `layer`). Works with Seurat v5
  and older. Needs the SeuratObject package.
- **`HyperCom_sce`** reads the `counts` assay by default (change with `assay`). Row names must be gene symbols. Data stored on disk
  (DelayedArray, HDF5Array) is read only for the database genes. Needs the SummarizedExperiment package, which comes with
  SingleCellExperiment (Bioconductor).

## 3. Ranked ligand-receptor pairs
`res$priority` has one table per weight, sorted from the highest priority. A pair ranks high when the cells that express its genes:

- are a large fraction of all cells, and each of its genes is expressed in many cells,
- send or receive the signal strongly,
- split evenly into senders and receivers,
- and, with `group`, concentrate in some groups (here SHAM or TAC).

There is one ranking for the whole dataset, not one per group.

With `significance=TRUE`, the tables also have p-values:

- **p:** the fraction of 1,000 background pairs of random genes that rank at least as high. It moves in steps of 0.001, and 0 means
  none did (report it as p < 0.001). Background pairs that get no priority are left out, with a warning.
- **p.adj:** p with the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment.
- To save time, pairs are first screened and only the pairs whose rank or p-value is in doubt are scored fully. The other
  priorities are estimates: typically within ~1e-9 of exact, up to ~1e-7 on the bundled data (1.5e-8 measured on the full bundled
  run). P-values and order are exact. `exact.priority=TRUE` gives exact values.

```{r}
head(res$priority[["1"]][, c("interaction", "priority", "p", "p.adj")])
```

`weights` sets how much the fraction of cells counts. The default, 1, weighs it like the other terms; smaller values favor pairs
specific to fewer cells. Several weights give one table each (see `prioritize_lr` below).

## 4. Score cells
```{r}
top <- res$priority[["1"]][1, ]
top.receptors <- unlist(top[grepl("^r[0-9]+$", colnames(top))])
top.receptors <- top.receptors[!is.na(top.receptors)]
```

The top pair is `r top$interaction` (ligand `r top$ligand`, receptor `r paste(top.receptors, collapse=" + ")`). `score_hypercom`
scores every cell for it:

- **`sender`, `receiver`:** from 0 to 1, how strongly the cell sends or receives the signal, compared with the other cells of its
  sample.
- **`dif`** = receiver - sender; **`avg`** is their mean; **`max`** the larger of the two.
- **`hypercom`:** one score per cell, negative for senders and positive for receivers.
- **NaN** (rare): the cell has no score, e.g. no path in the hypergraph to the pair's genes.

```{r}
top.scores <- score_hypercom(infMat=res$infMat, metadata=res$metadata, ligand=top$ligand,
                             receptors=top.receptors)
head(top.scores[, c("cell", "sender", "receiver", "max", "hypercom")])
```

How the scores are made: each pair of cells i and j of a sample gets a score for how strongly cell i reaches the ligand and the
receptor reaches cell j, relative to how strongly i reaches j. These scores are percent-ranked together. A cell's `sender` score is
its average rank as cell i, and its `receiver` score its average rank as cell j. `hypercom` is the sign of `dif` times the percent
rank of its size among the cells, times `avg`.

On the UMAP, senders are blue and receivers orange. Cells that express no ligand or receptor gene are not in the hypergraph and
stay grey.
```{r, eval=has.ggplot2}
umap <- data.frame(cell=rownames(cell.meta), UMAP_1=cell.meta$UMAP_1, UMAP_2=cell.meta$UMAP_2)
umap <- left_join(umap, top.scores[, c("cell", "hypercom")], by=join_by(cell))
ggplot(umap, aes(x=UMAP_1, y=UMAP_2, colour=hypercom)) +
  geom_point(size=0.5) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(low="#0074a7", mid="grey90", high="#e69c25", na.value="grey70") +
  ggtitle(top$interaction) +
  theme_classic()
```

Split by condition: the number of cells with the strongest sender and receiver scores (top 10% of `hypercom` at each end) in each
group, and the score distributions. `res$metadata` comes from `generate_metadata`, which names the column given as `group`
(here `condition`) `group`, and the one given as `sample` `sample`.
```{r}
top.scores <- left_join(top.scores, res$metadata, by=join_by(cell))
cut.low <- quantile(top.scores$hypercom, 0.1, na.rm=TRUE)
cut.high <- quantile(top.scores$hypercom, 0.9, na.rm=TRUE)
table(droplevels(top.scores$group[top.scores$hypercom <= cut.low]), dnn="strongest senders")
table(droplevels(top.scores$group[top.scores$hypercom >= cut.high]), dnn="strongest receivers")
```

```{r, eval=has.ggridges, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
melt.scores <- pivot_longer(dplyr::select(top.scores, c(cell, group, sender, receiver)), !c(cell, group),
                            names_to="type", values_to="score")
ggplot(melt.scores, aes(x=score, y=type, fill=group)) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha=0.4) +
  xlab("Score") +
  ylab("Score type") +
  ggtitle(top$interaction) +
  theme_classic()
```

For a receptor complex, give all its subunits; their scores are averaged.
```{r}
Tgfb1_Tgfbr <- score_hypercom(infMat=res$infMat, metadata=res$metadata, ligand="Tgfb1",
                              receptors=c("Tgfbr1", "Tgfbr2"))
head(Tgfb1_Tgfbr[, c("cell", "sender", "receiver", "hypercom")])
```

## 5. Large data

### Run time and memory
Time and memory depend on the number of cells **per sample** (they grow with its square), so more samples of the same size cost
little. The data of this tutorial takes seconds. One sample, with p-values, 8 threads:

| Cells in the sample | Time | Memory needed |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 4 s | 0.5 GB |
| 3,000 | 34 s | 0.7 GB |
| 10,000 | 6 min | 1.5 GB |
| 30,000 | 53 min | 6.4 GB |
| 60,000 | 3.6 h | 21 GB |
| 100,000 | 10.5 h | 53 GB |

Measured with `HyperCom_seurat()` on one sample of a Xenium 5K human ovarian cancer slide, with the CellChat human database
(about 700 pairs expressed) and `significance=TRUE`: HyperCom 0.3.1 on a cluster node (Intel Xeon Gold 6326, 8 cores), median of 5
runs (3 at 60,000 and 100,000 cells). "Memory needed": peak memory with `memory.gb` just above HyperCom's own estimate. GB = 10^9^
bytes.

- **More memory, faster:** HyperCom fits its scoring to the memory it has and is up to 1.4× faster when it has more: 10,000
  cells in 4.4 min with 2.7 GB, 30,000 in 38 min with 15 GB, 60,000 in 2.8 h with 57 GB (no `memory.gb` limit, 64 GiB job).
- **Pairs:** time also grows with the number of ligand-receptor pairs expressed (about 700 here).
- **P-values** (1,000 background pairs) take about two thirds of the time. HyperCom also screens the real pairs when it computes
  p-values.

### Where the memory goes
- **Scoring the pairs** takes most of the memory: about 17.6 bytes for every pair of cells in the same sample, plus about 1.1 GB
  for the rest of the run. The number of such pairs is the sum over samples of the squared number of cells, so before a run you
  can estimate the memory in GB with
  `sum(as.numeric(table(metadata$sample))^2) * 17.6 / 1e9 + 1.1` (an upper bound: only cells that express a ligand or receptor
  gene count).
- **The influence matrix** is kept, with the default `infmat.method="woodbury"`, as smaller pieces from which any entry can be
  computed, so its memory grows with the number of cells, not its square. When there are at least as many hyperedges (of two or
  more nodes) as nodes, that is, no more cells than interactions of two or more distinct genes, all expressed, the full matrix is
  made instead, as it is then no bigger. The bundled 1,000 cells stay factored (1,661 hyperedges, 1,663 nodes).
  `infmat.method="lu"` always makes the full matrix, with exactly the numbers of the original release of HyperCom (0.0.0.9000), and
  needs two matrices of all cells and genes squared.

### Fitting the memory
- **Automatic.** Before scoring, HyperCom compares its estimate with `memory.gb` (default: 90% of the computer's memory, or of a
  container's or cluster job's limit on Linux). If the fastest scoring does not fit, it uses a leaner one: about 5.5 bytes per pair
  of cells instead of 17.6, up to 1.4× slower, with priorities within ~1e-11. About 100,000 cells in one sample fit in 64 GB.
  With `verbose=TRUE` you see e.g. `Scoring needs at most about 56.5 GB of memory (memory mode; exact scoring would need 177 GB)`.
  If even that does not fit, the run stops at once, giving the estimate. The estimate is an upper bound with a floor of about
  1.1 GB, so small runs report about 1.08 GB while using less, and `memory.gb` below that always stops.
- **On a cluster, give the job's memory.** For a job that asks for 64 GB, pass `memory.gb=64`: the computer may have more memory
  than the job may use.
- **The leaner scoring needs the default `infmat.method="woodbury"`.**
- **"... cells and ... genes are not connected to the rest of the hypergraph and are left out".** This warning counts cells and
  genes that no chain of shared genes and interactions links to the rest (e.g. cells that express only the genes of an interaction
  that shares no gene with any other). They could neither send nor receive anything, so they get no scores. A few are normal; if
  many cells are left out, check the database species and the gene names.
- **`score_hypercom` on big runs** needs as much memory as the run's scoring and fits it the same way: give it the
  same `memory.gb`. Each call recomputes the within-sample influence values, so on large data each call takes a while.
- **Splitting a sample into more samples** saves memory but changes which cells are compared, and so the results.

### Runs that stop
Scoring the pairs takes almost all the time: hours on large data. As it goes, HyperCom saves the scored pairs in
`<outdir>/6.priority/cache`. **If a run stops** (cluster time limit, crash, closed R session), **run the same call again.** The
earlier steps repeat (seconds) and scoring continues from the cache, losing at most the last batch of pairs. Each scoring step
that finds pairs in the cache says so on its own line, e.g. for a run with p-values stopped while screening the background pairs:

```
  Continuing from the cache in overview/6.priority/cache: 1042 of 1042 real pairs already screened
  Continuing from the cache in overview/6.priority/cache: 343 of 1000 background pairs already screened
```

Without p-values the line ends in `pairs already scored`.

- **Same results** as a run that never stopped, on the same type of computer. Another CPU can change the last digits (about
  1e-13), so on a cluster ask for the same node type. Without `seed`, the run keeps the background pairs it drew before the stop.
  `weights` and `threads` may change between the calls.
- **The cache is deleted** once the priority files are written.
- **The cache is not used**, but moved to `cache.old` with a warning that says why, when the second call differs in: the counts,
  the database, the cells' sample or group, `r` or `infmat.method`; the kind of scoring (fastest or leaner, which follows
  `memory.gb` and the computer's memory); or the version of HyperCom. A damaged cache is moved aside too. Rename `cache.old` back to
  continue the run it belongs to.
- **If the cache cannot be written** (e.g. a full disk), scoring goes on without it. `resume=FALSE` turns it off.
- `prioritize_lr` keeps its cache in `<outdir>/cache`, and none with `outdir=NULL`.

On a cluster, a job can therefore ask for less time than the whole run. Submit the same script again until it finishes:
```{r, eval=FALSE}
res <- HyperCom(lrdb=lrdb, counts=counts, metadata=cell.meta,
                sample="sample", group="condition", significance=TRUE, seed=1,
                memory.gb=64, outdir="overview")
```

## 6. Step by step: how HyperCom works
This section runs each step of `HyperCom` on its own, with `outfile=NULL` (and `outdir=NULL` for `prioritize_lr`) so nothing is
written.

### Filter the counts
To save memory, keep only the genes of the database that are expressed (above 0). The matrix is also transposed to cells x genes.
```{r}
lr.counts <- filter_counts(counts=counts, lrdb=lrdb, outfile=NULL)
dim(lr.counts)
```

Then keep only the interactions whose genes are all expressed.
```{r}
lrs <- generate_lrs_table(counts=lr.counts, lrdb=lrdb, outfile=NULL)
dim(lrs)
```

### Build the hypergraph
A hyperedge links any number of nodes. HyperCom makes two types:

1. **expression edges:** a ligand or receptor gene and the cells that express it,
2. **interaction edges:** the genes of one ligand-receptor interaction.

They are stored as a data frame with an edge and a node column (a node belongs to that edge), each edge with weight 1. Cells and
genes not connected to the rest are left out (see section 5).
```{r}
hyperedges <- generate_hyperedges(counts=lr.counts, lrs=lrs, outfile=NULL)
head(hyperedges, 2)
```

The adjacency matrix has the cells, ligand genes and receptor genes as nodes; each entry is the number of hyperedges two nodes
share. It is not stored in full: `adj` keeps which nodes are in which hyperedge, which is much smaller, and works like a matrix
(`dim(adj)`, `adj[i, j]`, `as.matrix(adj)` for the whole matrix).
```{r}
adj <- generate_adjacency_matrix(hyperedges=hyperedges, outfile=NULL)
dim(adj)
adj[c("Thbs1", "Sdc4"), 1:3]
```

### Compute the influence matrix
A random walk with restart on the adjacency matrix gives the influence matrix: entry (i, j) is the share of a walk started at node
i that ends at node j, so each row sums to 1. At every step the walk returns to its start with the restart probability `r`, so
about `r` of each node's influence stays on itself and the rest spreads over the nodes it shares hyperedges with.
`generate_infMat` and `HyperCom` take `r` (default 0.5). Like `adj`, `infMat` works like a matrix without being stored in full
(section 5).
```{r}
infMat <- generate_infMat(adj=adj, r=0.5, outfile=NULL)
dim(infMat)
infMat[c("Thbs1", "Sdc4"), 1:3]
```

### Prepare the metadata
The matrices now have genes as well as cells, so the metadata gets a row per gene too, with `"gene"` in each column. To save
memory, only the cell, sample and group columns are kept; `keep` adds others.
```{r}
node.meta <- generate_metadata(infMat=infMat, metadata=cell.meta,
                               sample="sample", group="condition",
                               keep=NULL, outfile=NULL)
head(node.meta)
```

### Rank the pairs
`prioritize_lr` ranks the pairs (section 3). The priority is the weighted geometric mean of five terms of the cells that express
the pair's genes:

| Term | What it measures |
|---|---|
| `frac` | their fraction of all cells (its weight is `weights`; the others have weight 1) |
| `pct.min` | the smallest fraction of cells expressing one of the pair's genes |
| `max` | the mean of each cell's larger score, as sender or as receiver |
| `balance` | how evenly they split into senders and receivers |
| `purity` | how concentrated they are in some groups (1 without `group`; 0, and so priority 0, when spread exactly evenly) |

Here two weights give two tables.
```{r}
priority <- prioritize_lr(lrs=lrs, adj=adj, infMat=infMat, metadata=node.meta,
                          weights=c(1, 0.5), outdir=NULL,
                          verbose=FALSE)
head(priority[["1"]])
```
